prompt: What is monetary policy?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Interest-rate, money-supply and credit policy

options.label: C
options.text: Training and infrastructure investment to expand productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Tariffs and quotas

explanation: Monetary policy uses monetary instruments to influence aggregate demand. Fiscal policy uses spending and taxation, while supply-side and protectionist measures are different policy categories.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: The competition authority

options.label: D
options.text: The customs agency

options.text: Government capital spending

options.label: D

prompt: A central bank reduces its policy interest rate. This action is normally classified as

options.label: D

options.label: A
options.text: Expansionary monetary policy

options.label: B
options.text: Expansionary supply-side policy

options.label: C
options.text: Contractionary fiscal policy

options.label: D
options.text: Contractionary monetary policy

options.label: A

options.text: Expansionary monetary policy

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: A

options.label: D

prompt: What is meant by easing credit regulations?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing direct taxation on borrowers

options.label: D

prompt: An economy has rapid demand-pull inflation and very low unemployment. Which monetary response and mechanism is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise rates to restrain consumption and investment and shift AD left

options.label: B
options.text: Lower interest rates to restrain consumption and investment and shift AD left through cheaper borrowing

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the money supply to reduce price pressure by lowering household and business spending

options.label: D
options.text: Ease credit regulations to reduce borrowing and shift AD left through tighter lending conditions

prompt: Why might a rise in interest rates have only a small effect on aggregate demand?

options.label: A
options.text: A higher rate always increases consumption because households receive more interest income

options.label: B
options.text: Consumption and investment may be relatively insensitive to borrowing costs

options.label: C
options.text: Interest rates affect only government expenditure and not household or firm spending decisions

options.label: D
options.text: AD is fixed by definition and therefore cannot respond to monetary policy

explanation: The strength of monetary policy depends on behavioural responses. If households and firms do not change spending much when rates rise, AD falls only slightly.
reference: 5.3 Monetary policy | 5.3.2 tools of monetary policy: interest rates, money supply and credit regulations | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why might a fall in interest rates have only a small effect on aggregate demand during a period of very weak confidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Households and firms may not borrow or spend more despite cheaper credit

options.label: B
options.text: Lower rates necessarily reduce the money supply enough to offset any change in private spending

options.label: C
options.text: The fall in rates automatically raises taxes and reduces disposable income by the same amount

options.label: D
options.text: Credit becomes legally unavailable whenever the policy interest rate is reduced

explanation: Cheaper borrowing does not guarantee greater expenditure. Pessimistic households and firms may postpone spending and investment.
reference: 5.3 Monetary policy | 5.3.2 tools of monetary policy: interest rates, money supply and credit regulations | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why might easing credit regulations fail to produce a large rise in aggregate demand?

options.label: A
options.text: Easier credit always lowers AD by reducing household and business borrowing

options.label: B
options.text: Commercial banks must stop lending when regulations are eased because lending becomes prohibited

options.label: C
options.text: Borrowers may not want more credit even when access improves

options.label: D
options.text: The policy directly reduces government spending and therefore shifts AD left

explanation: The policy increases access to credit, but the final spending response also depends on willingness to borrow and confidence.
reference: 5.3 Monetary policy | 5.3.2 tools of monetary policy: interest rates, money supply and credit regulations | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can expansionary monetary policy create a stronger inflationary effect as the economy approaches full capacity?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand shifts left automatically as the economy approaches capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Supply responds less to demand

options.label: C
options.text: Rates cease to be tools

options.label: D
options.text: Bank lending regulations become fiscal instruments near full capacity

explanation: As spare capacity disappears, firms find it harder to increase output. Additional AD therefore produces proportionately more price-level pressure.

prompt: Which sequence best describes the full short-run effect of a clearly contractionary monetary package?

options.label: B

prompt: A central bank wants to raise employment using expansionary monetary policy. Which condition most increases the chance that the policy will raise real output rather than mainly prices?
